data.title: Chip stocks recover most of a 8.0% early slide; Nasdaq ends down 0.6%
data.description:
Chip stocks recovered most of a steep early slide on Wednesday, November 25, 2026. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell as much as 8.0% in the morning and closed down 0.7% at 8,774.86, according to Nasdaq's index data, recovering about 92% of the early fall, by TECHi's calculation. The Nasdaq Composite closed down 0.6% at 23,585.80, after falling as much as 4.6%.

The ten AI hardware stocks TECHi tracks ended down 0.8% on average, after being down as much as 9.5% on average at their intraday lows. That leaves them 3.5% above their Friday closes, so the rally that followed Nvidia's reinstatement of Jensen Huang on Monday, which looked erased at the open, is partly intact at the close. Nvidia ended down 3.9% at $149.30.

How big was the recovery?

Large. At its low, the Nasdaq Composite was down 4.6%, at 22,632.40; it closed at 23,585.80, recovering about 87% of the fall from Tuesday's close, by TECHi's calculation. The semiconductor index recovered about 92% of its 8.0% drop. The S&P 500 closed down 0.3% after falling as much as 3.2%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average closed up 0.3% after being down as much as 2.2%.

The morning numbers had looked much worse. At 6 a.m., TECHi's pre-market board showed the ten hardware stocks down 5.1% on average, and at 9:51 a.m. they were down 7.7% and the Nasdaq 4.2%, as TECHi reported.

Which stocks recovered and which did not?

Super Micro and Dell did best among the ten, up 3.1% and up 0.6%. Micron and Arista Networks did worst, down 4.5% and down 2.7%. Micron had been down as much as 13.0% during the session, after Seoul's memory makers fell overnight, as TECHi reported. Three of the ten closed below their Friday levels: Broadcom, AMD and Arista Networks.

Nvidia was down as much as 9.1% during the day before closing down 3.9%. It is still 18.9% above its Friday close of $125.53, and its market value is about $3.60 trillion, using roughly 24.1 billion shares.

How has the week gone so far?

Up, down, and roughly flat. On Monday the ten hardware stocks rose an average of 13.6% after Nvidia's announcement; on Tuesday they fell 8.1%; on Wednesday they ended down 0.8%. Over the three sessions they are 3.5% above Friday's closes on average. The semiconductor index rose 14.0% on Monday, fell 7.9% on Tuesday and fell 0.7% on Wednesday, leaving it 4.4% above Friday's close.

Nvidia's three days were larger in both directions: up 31.5% on Monday, down 5.9% on Tuesday and down 3.9% on Wednesday, for a net gain of about 18.9% since Friday.

How did the close compare with the morning readings?

Much better. TECHi's 6 a.m. board showed the ten stocks down 5.1% from Tuesday's close and Nvidia at $147.60. They closed down 0.8%, and Nvidia at $149.30. On Monday the close also came in above the morning reading. Pre-market prices are thin, and this week they have been a poor guide to the close; in the three sessions before Monday, the close had come in below the morning reading instead.

What drove the morning fall?

A mix of tariff worries, inflation data and selling that began on Tuesday. Reuters reported on Tuesday that the administration was about to release the findings of a trade investigation into 16 economies, including Taiwan and South Korea, with new tariffs expected. The trade representative's office had still not posted any findings on its press release page by the close, according to TECHi's checks through the day. The PCE price index rose 3.8% from a year earlier in October, the Bureau of Economic Analysis said in the morning.

Without published tariff findings, the morning's selling was based on reports rather than an announced policy. TECHi did not find a specific announcement during the session that coincided with the recovery. The 10-year Treasury yield was at 4.868% late in the session, below Tuesday's 4.902%, a sign that some money stayed in bonds even as stocks recovered.

What happened to TSMC's US premium?

It widened again after Tuesday's low. TSMC's US shares closed at $342.34, down 2.0%. Against Wednesday's Taipei close of NT$2,150 and the central bank's closing rate of 33.126 Taiwan dollars per US dollar, five Taipei shares were worth about $324.52, so the US shares closed about 5.5% above them, by TECHi's calculation. On Tuesday the premium was 3.2%, its lowest in more than two years, as TECHi reported; its two-year median is 18.6%.

Where does November stand?

Still one of the weakest on record for the Nasdaq. From its October 30 close of 25,437.00, the Composite is down 7.3% for the month, by TECHi's calculation from Nasdaq's index history. That is better than the 10.6% fall at 9:51 a.m., but if the month ended here it would still be the Nasdaq's third-worst November since 2000, and its worst since 2008. Only Friday's shortened session remains.

The semiconductor index is down 17.9% for November, and the ten AI hardware stocks are down an average of 21.8% from their October 30 closes. Nvidia is down 27.0% for the month. The biggest November decliners among the ten are Marvell (33.3%), Micron (32.0%) and Dell (30.0%); Arista Networks has held up best, down 2.9%. Friday's session, which ends at 1 p.m., is the last chance for those monthly figures to change.

How did today's other TECHi subjects close?

HP Inc. closed up 11.5% at $31.15, a day after reporting PC revenue up 14% on 29% fewer units, as TECHi reported. Autodesk closed down 3.5% at $246.79, after a forecast that implies slower growth, as TECHi reported. Palantir closed up 1.5% at $163.59, after filings showed director Peter Thiel buying $122 million of its stock on November 20, as TECHi reported. Alphabet's Class A shares closed down 2.1% at $273.10, as TECHi tallied about $135 billion of fundraising this year.

For Nvidia, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's 10-day window for answers from the board ended on Wednesday with no public response, as TECHi reported.

What does it mean for shareholders?

That intraday prices this week have been a poor guide to where the day ends. Wednesday's open looked like a third straight day of heavy losses for chip stocks; the close was a modest decline. Holders who sold at the open locked in prices well below the close, and those who bought near the low did well.

The underlying questions have not changed: possible tariffs on the economies where chips are made, inflation that is still running near 4%, and an open investigation at Nvidia. Each could move the group sharply again, and the holiday leaves only one short session to react to anything that happens before Monday. The path matters as well as the result: a 13.6% rise, an 8.1% fall and an intraday slide of about 9.5% on Wednesday add up to a small net change, but swings of that size can trigger stop-loss orders and margin calls along the way, which can turn a paper loss into a real one for leveraged holders.

What to watch

US markets are closed on Thursday for Thanksgiving and close early, at 1 p.m., on Friday. Any tariff findings from the trade representative's office over the holiday. Asian markets on Thursday, which will trade without a US lead. Friday's close, which will settle November's figures for the Nasdaq. TECHi's Nvidia quote page carries the live price.

data.title: Applied Digital’s newest data center lease pays 18% more per megawatt than earlier ones
data.description:
Applied Digital's newest data center lease pays about $2.00 million a year for each megawatt of capacity, 18% more than the average of the company's five earlier leases, TECHi calculates from a lease-by-lease table in the investor presentation Applied Digital filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Wednesday evening. The 150-megawatt lease, signed with a tier-one investment-grade hyperscaler the company has not named and announced on Monday, is worth $5.40 billion over an 18-year base term.

Applied Digital's shares were up 6.8% at $13.13 in pre-market trading on Friday at 7:26 a.m. Eastern, according to Nasdaq data, after jumping 20.3% on Monday and falling 11.6% on Tuesday. They ended Wednesday 31% below their October 30 close and about 75% below their closing high of $49.65 on May 28. The same presentation shows how much of the contracted capacity is still being built and how the company plans to pay for it.

What does the new lease pay?

The presentation lists each of Applied Digital's six leases with its capacity, base term and expected base-term value. Dividing that value by the term gives an average annual rent, which is the method the company itself uses in the same document to estimate operating income for each site. For the new lease, $5.40 billion over 18 years works out to $300 million a year, or about $2.00 million for each of its 150 megawatts, TECHi calculates.

The company said in its Monday announcement that the lease has improved commercial terms over its prior leases, "including higher pricing". The table lets that claim be measured. The figures exclude pass-through power, so they cover the data center capacity rather than the electricity the tenant uses.

Delivery of the new capacity is expected to begin in the first half of 2028 and continue into the second half, and the company has not said where the campus will be. The lease is subject to conditions including approvals of a power supply agreement, according to the presentation.

How does it compare with the earlier leases?

The new lease is the most expensive in the portfolio on this measure. The two 300-megawatt leases at Polaris Forge 3 in North Dakota and Delta Forge 1 in Louisiana, both with high investment-grade hyperscalers, average about $1.67 million per megawatt a year, so the new lease pays 20% more. It pays 21% more than the 210-megawatt Delta Forge 2 lease in Alabama and 24% more than the two Polaris Forge 2 leases at Harwood, North Dakota, the lowest on the list.

CoreWeave's 400-megawatt lease at Ellendale, North Dakota, the only one in the portfolio with a tenant below investment grade, pays about $1.79 million per megawatt a year. That was more per megawatt than any of the investment-grade leases signed before this month, and the new lease pays 12% more again.

There is a limit to the comparison. Averages over a full term hide how the rent is set from year to year, and many data center leases rise by a fixed percentage each year. If that is the case here, an 18-year lease would show a higher average than a 15-year lease at the same starting rent, so part of the gap could come from the longer term rather than a higher price. The presentation does not give escalation terms, and TECHi cannot separate the two effects from the filing.

What would the lease earn against its cost?

Applied Digital expects a stabilized net operating income margin of 85%, plus or minus three points, at the new site, which gives about $255 million a year of net operating income once all the capacity is billing. The company estimates construction costs of $11 million to $13 million per megawatt across its campuses, which puts the new 150 megawatts at $1.65 billion to $1.95 billion.

On those figures, the new lease's yearly operating income would equal 13.1% to 15.5% of its construction cost, TECHi calculates, against 10.9% to 12.9% for Polaris Forge 3 and Delta Forge 1 and 12.1% to 14.3% for CoreWeave's lease. Net operating income is a non-GAAP measure that leaves out interest, depreciation and corporate costs, and the company describes all of these site figures as forward-looking and not guidance.

How much does Applied Digital still have to build?

Most of the contracted capacity is still being built. According to the presentation, 275 megawatts are operating and 1.285 gigawatts are under construction, with all of the contracted capacity due for delivery by 2028. At the company's own cost range, the 1,285 megawatts under construction would cost $14.1 billion to $16.7 billion in total, TECHi calculates, a figure that includes money already spent on sites under way. Applied Digital had $2.95 billion of cash at the end of August, according to its latest quarterly report.

The company plans to fund most of that with partners and project debt. Under a partnership of up to $5 billion with Macquarie Asset Management, Macquarie expects to invest $2.25 million of preferred equity per megawatt leased to investment-grade tenants, carrying a 12.75% dividend that can be paid in kind rather than cash for the first five years, and receives a 15% common stake in the Applied Digital subsidiary that holds those data centers, according to the presentation, which says parts of the arrangement are subject to final documentation. Project loans of up to 80% of cost cover most of the rest. For the new lease, that would mean about $338 million from Macquarie and $1.32 billion to $1.56 billion of debt, TECHi calculates.

Chief Financial Officer Saidal Mohmand said the company expects to complete the remaining project financing for Delta Forge 1 and Polaris Forge 3 in the first quarter of 2027, followed by Delta Forge 2 in the second quarter.

What did this week's financing filings add?

In a filing on Tuesday afternoon, Applied Digital said it had raised the size of its preferred equity purchase agreement with three B. Riley entities from $2.0 billion to $2.5 billion, leaving $1.035 billion available to draw. The agreement covers Series G convertible preferred stock, which can be converted into common shares. The amount still available equals about 28% of the company's market value at Wednesday's close, TECHi calculates from the 302.4 million shares outstanding on October 6, though the number of common shares it could become depends on conversion terms not set out in this filing.

The company also closed a $300 million bridge loan for Delta Forge 1. It is a 364-day delayed-draw term loan at the Secured Overnight Financing Rate plus three percentage points, and draws depend on conditions that include construction milestones and state commission approval of electrical rates. Applied Digital said it expects to seek additional financing to finish the Louisiana campus.

How have the shares traded this week?

Monday's 20.3% gain came on a day when the whole AI hardware group rose. Ten AI hardware stocks TECHi tracks gained 13.6% on average that day, when Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang, as TECHi reported, and CoreWeave, the tenant at Applied Digital's largest campus, rose 22.3%. On Tuesday Applied Digital fell 11.6% and CoreWeave 11.8%, and on Wednesday Applied Digital edged up 0.6%.

CoreWeave was up 5.7% at $45.00 before Friday's open. Through Wednesday, Applied Digital had lost 31.0% in November and CoreWeave 22.4%, against a 17.9% fall in the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, which at Wednesday's close was its second-worst November since 1999, as TECHi reported on Thursday.

At Wednesday's close, Applied Digital's market value was about $3.7 billion, and about $4.0 billion at Friday's pre-market price. That is small next to the $41.13 billion of contracted base-term rent, but the two numbers are not directly comparable: the rent arrives over 15 to 18 years, most of the buildings still have to be paid for, and lenders and preferred investors are paid before common shareholders.

What conditions still apply?

Several parts of the plan are not yet settled. Besides the power approvals for the new lease, a 100-megawatt expansion at Polaris Forge 2 is in negotiation and not signed, and the company's goal of 3.5 to 4 gigawatts of capacity by 2030 is not contracted, according to the presentation.

Applied Digital also signed a power purchase agreement on October 4 with Base Electron, an independent power producer it helped launch to build generation in its North Dakota region. Base Electron is partly owned and managed by some Applied Digital officers and directors in their own capacity, along with third parties, and Wes Cummins is chief executive of both companies; Applied Digital's board approved the agreement on the recommendation of a related-party committee, and Applied Digital shareholders own about 10% of Base Electron. Base Electron can end the agreement if financing for its plant has not closed by March 31, 2027, and the plant has not been built, the presentation says.

What to watch

  • Where the new 150-megawatt campus is, and whether its power supply agreement is approved.
  • Project financing for Delta Forge 1 and Polaris Forge 3, which the company expects in the first quarter of 2027, and for Delta Forge 2 in the second quarter.
  • Draws on the bridge loan and the B. Riley preferred facility, and the share count in Applied Digital's next quarterly report.
  • Whether the 100-megawatt Polaris Forge 2 expansion is signed.
  • Base Electron's financing deadline of March 31, 2027.
  • Friday's shortened session, which ends at 1 p.m. Eastern and settles November for the stock.

data.title: SK hynix’s Nasdaq shares trade 42% above Seoul as a reported U.S. plant stays undecided
data.description:
SK hynix's U.S.-listed shares were trading about 42% above the value of the Seoul shares they represent before Friday's open, TECHi calculates, on the morning the memory chipmaker told the Securities and Exchange Commission it had made no decision on a reported U.S. plant worth about 60 trillion won, or roughly $45 billion. Its American depositary shares, which trade on Nasdaq as SKHY, were at $117.74 at 8:32 a.m. Eastern, according to Nasdaq data, up 5.9% from Wednesday's close.

Each SKHY share represents one-tenth of a Seoul share. SK hynix closed at 1,110,000 won in Seoul on Friday, so one-tenth was worth about $83.13 at 1,335.24 won per dollar. In its filing, SK hynix said its U.S. subsidiary Solidigm is reviewing ways to expand production but that nothing had been decided, and it gave itself three months for its next update on the reported plant, after promising one within a month in October.

How large is the gap, and how long has it lasted?

The ADSs have traded above their Seoul value on every one of the 92 days both markets were open since SKHY began trading on July 10, TECHi calculates from Korea Exchange closing prices, Nasdaq closing prices and European Central Bank exchange rates. The gap ranged from 16% on July 27 to 62% on July 30, with a median of 39%. It has widened over time: the median was 31% in July and August and 45% so far in November.

That is far from where the shares started. The offering priced the ADSs at $149 on July 9, about 5% above the Seoul close used in the prospectus. The ADSs then closed at $168.01 on their first day, 16% above that day's Seoul value.

Daily readings jump around because the two markets do not trade at the same time. Seoul closes at 1:30 a.m. Eastern, more than 14 hours before Nasdaq, so news that arrives in between moves only one of the two prices. That is what happened on Monday. SK hynix closed 2.5% lower in Seoul, and hours later SKHY rose 20.0% in New York on a day when U.S. chip stocks jumped after Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang. The measured gap that day was 55%. In Seoul, SK hynix rose 6.7% on Tuesday.

Why doesn't the gap close?

When an ADS trades well above the shares behind it, traders usually buy the cheaper shares at home and deposit them to create new ADSs, which pushes the two prices together. SK hynix's prospectus says that route is controlled. The depositary needs the company's prior consent for any deposit that would take the shares held for ADSs above legal limits, the company's articles of incorporation or a maximum the company may set, and SK hynix can block deposits. The prospectus also warns that investors who swap their ADSs for Seoul shares may not be allowed to convert them back.

The supply of ADSs is also small. The July offering created 177.9 million ADSs, equal to 17.79 million common shares, which the prospectus put at about 2.5% of the company's issued shares. It said the size was capped so that SK square, SK hynix's largest shareholder, keeps at least 20% of the issued shares, as Korea's fair-trade law requires. Most of the company's value still trades in Seoul.

The gap is much wider than at TSMC, another large Asian chipmaker with U.S.-listed shares. TSMC's American depositary receipts traded 3.2% above their Taipei value on November 24, the lowest premium since at least August 2024, against a median of 18.6% over that period, as TECHi reported.

For a U.S. buyer, the gap has a cost. SK hynix's board declared a third-quarter dividend of 20,000 won per share on October 28, according to its quarterly report. A dividend of that size equals 1.80% of Friday's Seoul price. One ADS is entitled to a tenth of each share's dividend, which at Friday's exchange rate would be about $1.50, or 1.27% of the ADS price, before taxes and fees, TECHi calculates.

What did SK hynix say about the U.S. plant?

The Maeil Business Newspaper reported on October 29 that Solidigm, SK hynix's U.S. subsidiary, was pursuing an investment of about 60 trillion won to build a new NAND flash memory plant in the United States. The same day, SK hynix said in a filing that Solidigm was reviewing measures to strengthen its competitiveness and expand capacity but that nothing had been determined, and that it would update investors when details were confirmed or within one month.

Friday's filing repeats that nothing has been determined and sets a new limit of three months for the next update, which would fall by late February. The company did not name a site, a timetable or a cost of its own.

At 1,335.24 won per dollar, 60 trillion won is about $44.9 billion. For scale, SK hynix reported 42.7 trillion won of capital spending it had committed to but not yet recorded at the end of September, up from 6.7 trillion won at the end of 2025, and 156.7 trillion won of cash generated from operations in the first nine months of 2026, according to its quarterly report.

How much is SK hynix returning to shareholders?

On October 28, SK hynix announced shareholder returns of about 100 trillion won for fiscal 2026, made up of at least 30 trillion won of dividends and at least 60 trillion won of share buybacks and cancellations, according to the quarterly report. In an update filed on Wednesday, the company said those amounts include planned returns that may be decided or paid in 2027, and that it will use proceeds from its core business and from realized gains on investment assets. Its returns for 2025 were 14.3 trillion won.

At Friday's Seoul close, SK hynix's 706.8 million issued shares were worth about 785 trillion won, or $588 billion. The 100 trillion won plan equals about 12.7% of that value, and the buyback portion about 7.6%, TECHi calculates. The 60 trillion won reported for the plant matches the minimum set for buybacks.

How have the shares moved this week?

In Seoul, SK hynix fell 2.5% on Monday, rose 6.7% on Tuesday, fell 11.1% on Wednesday, as TECHi reported, and then gained 2.2% on Thursday and 5.4% on Friday, when Seoul's main index jumped. In New York, SKHY rose 20.0% on Monday, fell 9.9% on Tuesday and slipped 0.8% on Wednesday before the Thanksgiving break.

Since SKHY's first day of trading, SK hynix's Seoul shares have fallen 49%, while SKHY was down 30% at Friday's pre-market price. The won's 13% rise against the dollar over that period explains part of the difference, and the widening premium explains the rest.

What else is on SK hynix's calendar?

In a filing on November 20, SK hynix said it plans to acquire all of BCPE Pangea Cayman2, a company whose business is a stake in the former Toshiba memory business, now Kioxia, by converting bonds it holds, with the acquisition scheduled for December 4. Its quarterly report says the stake in Kioxia that SK hynix may hold, directly or indirectly, is limited to a certain percentage for a specified period.

What to watch

  • SK hynix's next disclosure on the reported Solidigm plant, due within three months of Friday.
  • Whether SKHY's premium to Seoul narrows when the regular U.S. session opens, in a day that closes at 1 p.m. Eastern.
  • The December 4 acquisition of BCPE Pangea Cayman2.
  • Fourth-quarter dividend and buyback decisions, which the company says its board sets each quarter based on the share price, market conditions and cash flow.
  • Seoul's Monday session, the first chance for SK hynix's home market to react to Friday's U.S. trading.

data.title: US tariff plan would exempt Taiwan-made servers; five suppliers hit Taipei’s limit
data.description:
The tariffs the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative proposed for Taiwan on Wednesday would not cover the computers and servers the island ships to American buyers. Taiwan's notice lists all 20 tariff subheadings for automatic data processing machines, the customs heading that includes servers, in an annex of products "not covered by the proposed action," next to server parts, network switches and chips. For other Taiwanese goods, the trade representative's announcement proposes a tariff of up to 15%, counted net of normal duties and existing Section 301 tariffs.

In Taipei on Thursday, with U.S. markets closed for Thanksgiving, eight server and network makers rose 7.2% on average and four parts suppliers 7.7%, while five of the twelve closed at Taiwan's 10% daily limit, according to Taiwan Stock Exchange data. TSMC, whose chips were already outside the proposal, slipped 0.2% to NT$2,145. The Taiex rose 2.8% to 39,262.39, still 2.1% below Tuesday's close.

What did the trade representative propose for Taiwan?

The announcement covers 14 of the 16 investigations the trade representative opened on March 11 into what it calls structural excess capacity in manufacturing. In each, it found the economy's practices "unreasonable" and a burden on U.S. commerce, which makes them actionable under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. Taiwan, South Korea, Japan, China, the European Union and nine others are on the list; Mexico and Norway have no determination yet.

For Taiwan, the notice proposes "tariffs on all goods of Taiwan of up to 15 percent, net of MFN rates and existing Section 301 tariffs." The same 15% figure applies to South Korea, Japan, the European Union and Switzerland, while the proposal for Vietnam goes up to 35% and the one for China up to 20%. If the trade representative finds that "ongoing consultations and commitments are unsatisfactory," the Taiwan notice offers a second option of up to 25%, net only of existing Section 301 tariffs.

Nothing takes effect yet. Comments and requests to testify are due January 5, 2027, and hearings begin January 25 at the U.S. International Trade Commission in Washington. The notice says the proposal accounts for Taiwan's reciprocal trade agreement with the United States, dated February 12, 2026. A Baker McKenzie summary adds a caution: the notices do not spell out how the "net of" formula would be calculated in practice.

Which products does the Taiwan notice leave out?

The notice lists four kinds of exemptions. The first covers goods already under Section 232 national security tariffs, including steel, aluminum and copper articles, cars and trucks and their parts, wood products, patented drugs and "semiconductor articles." The second covers books, donations and baggage. The third is the annex. The fourth is certain iron ores.

TECHi read the annex line by line. It holds 2,231 tariff subheadings, of which 971 carry no limit at all; the others apply only to a narrower use such as civil aircraft parts. Among the unlimited entries are all 20 subheadings of heading 8471, which covers computers, servers and storage units; the four subheadings for parts and circuit assemblies of those machines; switching and routing equipment; smartphones; 17 subheadings for diodes, transistors, LEDs and integrated circuits; and five for chipmaking machines.

Power supplies are treated differently. The 13 subheadings for transformers and power converters in heading 8504 appear only with an aircraft limit, so a power supply shipped for a data center would fall under the proposed tariff as written. The server, server-part, switch and integrated-circuit subheadings TECHi checked in South Korea's notice also appear there with no limits. Holland & Knight says the annexes in the 13 notices other than China's share a common baseline list.

How did Taipei trade on Thursday?

The day split along a clear line. The eight server and network makers in the table above rose 7.2% on average, and the four parts suppliers, which make power systems, cooling and circuit boards, rose 7.7%. The four chip companies rose 1.9% on average, held down by TSMC's small loss. Wistron, Wiwynn, Accton, Asia Vital Components and Unimicron each closed at the exchange's 10% limit.

The two-day picture is less lopsided. Every one of the sixteen stocks fell on Wednesday, when Taipei traded before Wall Street opened and before the trade representative's notices were in front of investors. Measured from Tuesday's close, the chip group is still down 6.1% on average and none of its four members is back above Tuesday's close, while the server group is up 0.7% and the parts group 3.2%. TSMC is 3.8% below Tuesday, MediaTek 8.5%.

Prices alone cannot say why. At least three things happened between Wednesday's Taipei close and Thursday's open: the notices, a Wall Street session in which the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index recovered most of an almost 8% fall, as TECHi reported, and a tightening of short-selling rules by Taiwan's Financial Supervisory Commission, according to the Taipei Times. Delta Electronics, whose power supplies appear in the annex only with the aircraft limit, still rose 6.2%, so the day was not a clean map of the tariff annex.

What does it mean for US AI hardware stocks?

Taiwan's contract manufacturers build servers, boards and network gear for U.S. cloud and AI companies, and those are the categories the annex leaves out. If the final notice keeps them there, the new duty would not land on those imports from Taiwan, whatever happens to the rate on other goods. Chips stay under the separate Section 232 regime that the notice cites, which this proposal does not add to.

That leaves the parts outside the annex, such as power equipment, plus any product the comment process moves on or off the list. The trade representative asks for comments on "the specific products to be subject to increased duties," so the list can still change before a final notice.

Friday is the first chance for U.S.-listed stocks to trade on all of this. TSMC's American depositary receipts last closed at $342.34 on Wednesday, before the Taipei session in which its local shares slipped, and the U.S. market closes early at 1 p.m. Eastern. On Tuesday the premium of those receipts over Taipei shares fell to its lowest since at least August 2024, as TECHi reported.

What has Taiwan's government said?

Executive Yuan spokeswoman Michelle Lee said on Wednesday that the recommended rates are not final decisions and that Washington must still hold hearings, according to the Taipei Times. She said the government was confident the final outcomes would reflect earlier bilateral negotiations. The paper quoted an unnamed source familiar with the talks who expects Taiwan's final rate to return to the agreed 15% ceiling that does not stack on normal duties.

The same report cited Chang Chien-yi, president of the Taiwan Institute of Economic Research, who estimated that the United States might add about 5 percentage points on top of the tariff Taiwan already pays under an earlier Section 301 action on forced labor, keeping the total at the 15% cap. He said the method of imposition had not been announced.

How did Seoul trade?

South Korea's notice proposes the same up to 15% rate, net of normal duties and existing Section 301 tariffs, with an alternative of up to 25%. South Korea already faces a Section 301 tariff from the July forced-labor action, which set rates of up to 12.5% for it and other economies, and the new proposal would bring the combined Section 301 rate on Korean goods to the 15% agreed in last year's trade deal, Yonhap reported. The agency also reported a U.S. warning that the rate could rise if concerns about Seoul's new chip-plant projects are not addressed; the trade representative's Korea report cites the K-Semiconductor Belt Strategy. Memory chips themselves fall under the semiconductor exemption. The KOSPI rose 0.29% to 4,711.21 on Thursday, giving back most of a 1.32% gain at 9:15 a.m. Seoul time reported by Yonhap, while Samsung Electronics rose 0.35% and SK hynix rose 2.23%, according to Korea Exchange prices. On Wednesday the KOSPI had fallen 6.2%, as TECHi reported.

What to watch

  • Friday's shortened U.S. session, the first trade in TSMC's receipts and in U.S. server and chip stocks since the notices and Asia's reaction.
  • The comment deadline on January 5 and the hearings from January 25, where companies can ask for products to be added to or taken off the annex.
  • The final notices, which will set the rate, the effective date and the final exemption list.
  • Determinations for Mexico and Norway, which the trade representative has not made yet.

data.title: Tempus will pay $600 million cash in Personalis deal, backed by a 9.4% Ares loan
data.description:
Tempus AI will pay about $600 million in cash for roughly a third of Personalis, the cancer-testing company it agreed to buy in July, and it has lined up a new $500 million loan package from Ares Capital to help cover it. Both moves are in a filing Tempus made after Wednesday's close. The cash portion is close to the $590 million in cash Tempus reported at the end of September.

The choice swaps new Tempus shares for debt. At Wednesday's Tempus price, paying cash for 36.9 million Personalis shares means issuing about 11 million fewer Tempus shares, TECHi calculates from the merger terms. The term loan costs SOFR plus 5.5 percentage points, or about 9.44% at the latest rate published by the New York Fed, which works out to roughly $36 million a year if the full $385 million is drawn.

What did Tempus decide?

Under the July 20 merger agreement, each Personalis share is worth $16.25, paid mostly in Tempus stock, and Tempus could choose to pay cash for up to half of the shares. On November 24, Tempus told Personalis it would pay cash for 36,923,077 shares. Based on 108,740,631 Personalis shares outstanding, that is 34.0% of the company and about $600 million.

Every Personalis holder gets the same mix. For each share, a holder receives $16.25 in cash on about 34% of the position and Tempus stock on the rest, according to the agreement. On a holding of 100 shares, that is about $552 in cash for 34 shares plus roughly 19.6 Tempus shares for the other 66, if the ratio were set at Wednesday's Tempus price, TECHi calculates. Together that is worth about $1,625, or $16.25 a share, as long as Tempus stays above the floor. Tempus said the cash share number can be reduced automatically to keep the deal's tax treatment as a reorganization, in which case more of the payment would come in stock.

The deal still needs a vote. Personalis holders meet on November 30, and proxy advisers ISS and Glass Lewis have both recommended voting in favor, Personalis said in a November 23 filing. The companies expect to close in early December.

What is Tempus buying?

Personalis makes NeXT Personal, a blood test that looks for traces of cancer left after treatment, known as molecular residual disease. Tempus already sold that test under a partnership that began in November 2023, when it also invested in Personalis, and its July announcement put the deal's enterprise value at $1.5 billion, net of the stake Tempus already owns. Tempus called residual-disease testing a $20 billion market.

Personalis is much smaller than its buyer and still loses money. It reported $25.6 million of revenue in the September quarter and $63.4 million over nine months, with a nine-month net loss of $95.5 million and $98.3 million of cash at September 30, according to its quarterly filings. Tempus's own September-quarter revenue was about 16 times larger.

The market did not cheer the deal on the day. Personalis fell 13.3% to $13.34 on July 20, even though $16.25 was 5.6% above its previous close, and Tempus fell 7.7% to $48.41, Nasdaq data show.

How is Tempus paying for it?

The Ares credit agreement, signed on Wednesday, provides a $385 million senior secured term loan and a $115 million revolving credit line. Tempus can draw the money only when the Personalis deal closes or is about to close within one business day, and it plans to use it for part of the cash consideration, deal costs and general purposes.

Interest on both pieces must be paid in cash rather than added to the balance, and the revolver is limited by a borrowing base made up of eligible receivables and certain cash, so Tempus may not be able to draw all of it at once. Term loans carry interest at SOFR plus 5.50% or a base rate plus 4.50%, with a 1% floor on SOFR, and the revolver costs SOFR plus 3.75%. Tempus has to pay interest on at least the greater of half the revolver or $57.5 million, even if it borrows less. At the latest SOFR, that minimum alone costs about $4.4 million a year at the revolver's rate of 7.69%. The loans mature in five years, but the maturity jumps forward to 91 days before Tempus's 0.75% convertible notes due 2030 come due, unless those notes are repaid or converted first or Tempus meets a liquidity test.

Why does the Tempus share price matter?

The stock part of the deal is not fixed in shares. If Tempus's 15-day average price before closing is above $48.42, Personalis holders get $16.25 worth of Tempus stock for each share paid in stock. If it falls to $48.42 or below, the ratio locks at 0.3356 Tempus shares, and the value of the stock part falls with the price.

That floor is now in view. Tempus closed at $54.74 on Wednesday, 13.1% above the floor, and 35.7% below its highest close since the deal was signed, $85.08 on September 28, according to Nasdaq data. When the deal was signed, Tempus closed at $48.41 on July 20, just under where the floor sits.

Personalis closed at $14.11, 15.2% below the $16.25 value, with the vote four days away and closing expected within weeks. The math below the floor is simple. If Tempus averaged $45 before closing, the stock part would be worth about $15.10 a share, and with the cash part each Personalis share would be worth roughly $15.49, TECHi calculates. That is still above Wednesday's Personalis price, but the cushion would shrink with every further drop in Tempus.

A gap that wide on a deal this close to completion suggests traders see some risk in the stock leg, the timing or the vote, though prices alone do not say which. The cash election narrows that risk for Personalis holders, because a third of each holding is now paid at a fixed $16.25.

What does it mean for Tempus shareholders?

The cash election trades dilution for leverage. At Wednesday's price, an all-stock deal would have meant issuing about 32 million Tempus shares, while the new mix means about 21 million. The exact number depends on the average price before closing.

The cost of that choice is interest. A 9.44% rate on the full term loan compares with the 0.75% coupon on Tempus's convertible notes due 2030, and Tempus reported about $176 million of noncurrent convertible debt at September 30. It also reported $412 million of revenue in the September quarter. TECHi's November 2 report on Tempus's 2027 forecast noted that the company said regulatory review of the deal had cleared, leaving the shareholder vote and other closing conditions.

Whether the swap pays off depends on the price Tempus stock would have fetched. Paying cash at $16.25 a share instead of issuing stock is cheaper for existing holders if Tempus shares later trade above the level at which the shares would have been issued, and dearer if they keep falling.

What to watch

  • The Personalis vote on November 30 and the closing in early December.
  • Tempus's average share price before closing, against the $48.42 floor.
  • How much of the term loan and revolver Tempus draws at closing, and whether it uses the revolver beyond the $57.5 million on which it pays interest regardless.
  • Personalis's discount to $16.25 when trading resumes on Friday.
  • Tempus's share price on Friday's shortened session.

data.title: ASML rises 3.2% in Amsterdam as US tariff plan leaves chipmaking machines out
data.description:
Shares of ASML, the Dutch maker of the lithography machines used to make advanced AI chips, rose 3.2% in Amsterdam on Thursday to €1,168.20, the first full European session after the U.S. trade representative proposed new tariffs on goods from the European Union. The EU notice lists all five tariff subheadings for semiconductor-manufacturing machines, heading 8486, among products "not covered by the proposed action," with no limits attached.

The rest of Europe's chip-equipment group moved the same way. ASM International rose 3.2%, BE Semiconductor Industries 3.0% and chipmaker Infineon 3.6%, while the STOXX Europe 600 technology index rose 2.9%, according to exchange data. U.S. markets were closed for Thanksgiving, so ASML's Nasdaq-listed shares last traded on Wednesday at $1,303.08, 1.6% above the dollar value of Thursday's Amsterdam close at the European Central Bank's reference rate, TECHi calculates.

What did the trade representative propose for the EU?

The European Union is one of 14 economies the trade representative found to have "unreasonable" practices tied to excess manufacturing capacity in its announcement on Wednesday. For the EU, the notice proposes "a tariff rate of 15 percent, net of MFN rates and existing Section 301 tariffs," with exemptions, which is the same rate proposed for Taiwan, South Korea, Japan and Switzerland.

If the trade representative decides that talks and existing commitments are unsatisfactory, the notice offers an alternative of up to 20%. It says the proposal accounts for the U.S.-EU framework agreement on trade and proposes that the adjustment end on December 1, 2028, in line with two EU regulations cited in the notice. Comments are due January 5, 2027, and hearings begin January 25.

The notice says that end date is consistent with the terms of two EU regulations from this year, numbered 2026/1455 and 2026/1422. TECHi has not reviewed those regulations, so the reason for the date is not clear from the notice alone, and it is a detail worth watching as the comment period runs.

Which chipmaking machines are exempt?

Heading 8486 covers the machines and parts used to make chips and displays. The EU notice's annex lists all five of its subheadings with no scope limits: machines for making boules or wafers; machines for making semiconductor devices or integrated circuits; machines for flat-panel displays; machines for masks and reticles and for chip assembly; and parts and accessories for all of them.

Lithography systems such as ASML's fall under the second of those, the heading for machines that make semiconductor devices and integrated circuits. The same annex also lists servers and integrated circuits with no limits, and semiconductor articles already under Section 232 tariffs are excluded by the notice's general exemption. Taiwan's notice uses the same baseline list, as TECHi reported on Thursday morning.

Who else in Europe makes chip equipment?

ASML is the largest of a small group of European companies that sell tools to chipmakers. ASM International, also based in the Netherlands, makes deposition equipment that lays down the thin films used in advanced chips. BE Semiconductor Industries makes packaging and bonding machines, including the hybrid-bonding tools used to stack chips together. Germany's Infineon is a chipmaker rather than a toolmaker, best known for power semiconductors.

All four rose on Thursday, but their U.S. exposure differs. Equipment makers ship machines to chip plants, which the EU notice exempts by heading. Chips themselves are exempt from this action both through the annex and through the notice's carve-out for goods already under Section 232 tariffs.

How did Europe's chip stocks trade?

Thursday's moves made up only part of the ground lost earlier in the week. ASML closed at €1,168.20, against €1,131.60 on Wednesday, and the STOXX Europe 600 rose 1.8%, while Amsterdam's AEX index gained 1.9%. The technology index's 2.9% rise outpaced the broad market by about 1.0 percentage points. Europe's markets close at 11:30 a.m. Eastern time, before most of Wednesday's U.S. session played out, so Thursday's gains may also reflect the U.S. recovery that came after Europe had closed on Wednesday.

Prices alone do not say how much of the move came from the tariff notice. The proposed 15% rate is in line with the cap in the U.S.-EU framework agreement, according to an analysis by Holland & Knight, so the headline rate was less of a surprise than the detail of the exemptions. The chip-equipment exemption covers the machines ASML ships to chip plants in the United States.

Why does the exemption matter for U.S. chip plants?

ASML is the only company that makes extreme ultraviolet lithography machines, the tools needed to print the most advanced chips. Every new leading-edge factory in the United States, including those being built by TSMC, Intel, Samsung and Micron, depends on them. A tariff on those machines would have added to the cost of plants that the U.S. government has been subsidizing.

The exemption keeps that cost out of the proposal, at least for now. The trade representative asks for comments on which products should be added to or removed from the annex, so the list of exempt goods could still change before a final notice is issued.

What does it mean for ASML's US shares?

ASML's Nasdaq-listed shares closed at $1,303.08 on Wednesday, down 2.5% on the day. Converted at the ECB's reference rate of 1.0975 dollars per euro, Thursday's Amsterdam close equals about $1,282.10, 1.6% below the U.S. close, TECHi calculates. Each Nasdaq share represents one ordinary share.

That gap is a rough guide rather than a forecast. The ECB sets its reference rate once a day, earlier in the afternoon than the Amsterdam close, so the conversion is a snapshot rather than the exchange rate at the moment trading ended. The two markets usually track each other closely, but exchange rates and Friday's European session, which ends before the shortened U.S. session closes at 1 p.m. Eastern, can move the comparison again. ASML's U.S. shares are down 16.8% in November so far, from $1,565.90 on October 30, a month in which the chip index has had its second-worst November since 1999, as TECHi reported.

How has ASML traded this month?

ASML's U.S. shares have swung with the rest of the chip sector in November. They closed at $1,266.22 on November 20, jumped to $1,383.78 on November 23, the day Nvidia reinstated its chief executive, and then gave back ground on the following two days, according to Nasdaq data. From the October 30 close of $1,565.90, that leaves the U.S. shares 16.8% lower for the month, slightly less than the chip index's 17.9% fall over the same period.

For other European goods, the proposal works differently. Cars and car parts, steel and aluminum products, wood products and patented medicines that already face Section 232 tariffs are excluded from this action, as are the products in the annex. Most other EU goods would face the proposed rate of up to 15%, net of normal duties and existing Section 301 tariffs, if the plan is adopted as written.

What to watch

  • Friday's shortened U.S. session, the first trade in ASML's Nasdaq shares since the EU notice.
  • Comments due January 5 and hearings from January 25, where the list of exempt goods could change.
  • Whether the European Commission responds formally to the proposal and to the alternative 20% rate.
  • ASM International, BE Semiconductor and Infineon in Friday's European session, for signs of whether Thursday's gains hold.
  • The final notice, which will set the rate, the effective date and the exemption list.

data.title: Blaize says 18 months of results can’t be relied on; China was 88% of the revenue
data.description:
Blaize, a Nasdaq-listed maker of AI chips and servers, told investors after Wednesday's close that its financial statements for all of 2025 and the first half of 2026 should no longer be relied on. In an 8-K filing accepted at 4:15 p.m. Eastern, the San Jose company said its audit committee reached that conclusion on November 23 after reviewing revenue, "primarily revenue derived from agreements with the Company's customers in China," as part of an internal investigation.

TECHi added up what is at stake from the company's own reports. Blaize recorded $53.4 million of revenue in 2025 and the first half of 2026, the span those statements cover, and $47.1 million of it, or 88%, came from customers shipping to China, according to the geographic tables in its annual report and its June-quarter report. One customer, identified only as Customer D, accounted for $35.7 million, or 67%.

What did Blaize disclose on Wednesday?

The filing lists the statements that are now unreliable: the audited results for the year ended December 31, 2025, and the unaudited results for the quarters ended March 31, June 30 and September 30, 2025, and March 31 and June 30, 2026. The company said it will file restated statements "as soon as practicable" and gave no estimate of how large the changes will be.

The trigger was an outside inquiry. In July and August, the Department of Justice sent subpoenas and requests to the company and some of its employees and board members, seeking information about "the Company's business and agreements with certain counterparties," and the Securities and Exchange Commission asked for similar information on a voluntary basis, Blaize has said. Its board set up a special committee to run an internal investigation with independent advisers, and management then reviewed the revenue it had booked. The audit committee discussed the decision with the company's auditor, UHY LLP.

Blaize also said it has not finished assessing what the restatement means for its internal control over financial reporting and its disclosure controls. It said it will not reach a final conclusion on those controls until the restatement is complete. The filing does not say how the misstatements are spread across periods or customers, or whether any revenue will move from one period to another.

How much of Blaize's revenue came from China?

Almost all of it, once the business took off. In 2024, Blaize recorded $1.6 million of revenue and none of it from China. Revenue jumped about 25-fold to $38.6 million in 2025, and the China share rose from 32% in the first half to 96% in the second. The fourth quarter alone brought in $23.8 million, or 62% of the year.

The pattern carried into 2026. The first quarter had $2.7 million of revenue and no sales to China, then the second quarter brought $12.0 million, with 100% of it from China. TECHi derived the second-half 2025 and first-quarter 2026 figures by subtracting the company's half-year and quarterly totals from its annual and half-year totals.

The filings name three counterparties tied to that business. Blaize signed a strategic cooperation agreement in 2025 with Starshine Computing Power Technology, a Hong Kong company that agreed to deliver at least $120 million of revenue over 18 months, subject to purchase orders; the company said in August it did not expect further orders from Starshine. A customer called BST placed one order in the second quarter of 2025. NeoTensr placed a $23.8 million order in the fourth quarter of 2025, which Blaize said was paid in full during 2026, and signed a contract in April for up to $50 million over a year.

The filings do not say which lettered customer is which, so TECHi does not link Customer D to a name. Blaize's own disclosures do show that Customer D was its only customer of size in the June quarter, at $11.9 million.

What happened to the money?

Some of it has not arrived. At the end of June, NeoTensr owed Blaize $13.3 million under the April contract, due September 24. On October 5, the company said NeoTensr had paid $0.2 million of that and that it had agreed to extend the terms, with payment expected during the fourth quarter. In August the contract was amended into a take-or-pay arrangement, with server deliveries running through July 2027.

Blaize raised about $32.8 million, after fees, in a share sale in the second quarter of 2026, its only capital raise in the first half, and used $41.3 million of cash in its operations over those six months. It had $36.8 million of cash at June 30, and said about 34% of its cash balance sat in Chinese banks subject to currency controls that could delay moving it out. It lost $206.9 million in 2025 and $51.5 million in the first half of 2026, In its June-quarter report it said its ability to continue as a going concern depends on several factors, and that it cannot draw on a committed equity facility, with about $15.5 million left, while its share price is below $1.

The October filing also set expectations low for the rest of the year. Blaize said third-quarter revenue would be about $0.5 million, all from one customer in Europe, and revised its 2026 revenue forecast to between $32 million and $36 million, based on NeoTensr orders and one more order that was awaiting signature.

How has the stock traded?

Blaize shares closed at $0.147 on Wednesday, up 11.9% in the regular session that ended before the filing, according to Nasdaq data. After hours they changed hands at the same price on about 16,214 shares, a thin market that says little about Friday. At Wednesday's price, the 144.8 million shares outstanding in August were worth about $21 million. The stock is down 97.8% from an intraday high of $6.76 on October 15, 2025.

Nasdaq told the company on September 28 that its shares had closed below $1 for 30 straight business days, and Blaize has until March 29, 2027, to regain compliance. Its quarterly report for the September quarter is also late: in a notice on November 17, Blaize said it could not file by the November 16 deadline and did not expect to file within the five-day extension.

What else is pending?

Two shareholder lawsuits are already open in federal court in California. The first, filed on August 4, covers investors who bought between July 18, 2025, and April 28, 2026, and claims the company made misleading statements about its contracts with Starshine and NeoTensr. The second, filed on September 17, also names the underwriters of a May 2026 share offering.

The company has changed its finance leadership during the review. Martin Costas, a former finance chief at BOXABL and at a Honeywell unit, became chief financial officer and chief operations officer on November 2.

The restatement leaves the central question open: whether revenue booked from China moves to other periods, shrinks, or disappears, and whether the change reaches the cash the company has already collected.

What to watch

  • The restated statements and the late September-quarter report, which will show how much revenue changes and in which periods.
  • Any Nasdaq notice about the late quarterly report, on top of the minimum-price deficiency.
  • Whether NeoTensr pays the extended $13.1 million balance in the fourth quarter.
  • Developments in the Justice Department and SEC inquiries and in the two class actions.
  • Friday's shortened session, the first regular trading since the filing.

data.title: Autodesk paid $3.66 billion for MaintainX; its new revenue line rose $35 million
data.description:
Autodesk's quarterly report, filed after Wednesday's close, gives the first look at what its MaintainX purchase is bringing in. A new revenue line called "Other products," which includes the MaintainX maintenance software Autodesk bought in August, rose by $35 million from a year earlier to $135 million in the three months to October 31, and the company said the increase was "primarily due to revenue from MaintainX," according to the 10-Q filing.

The price was far larger. Autodesk paid $3.66 billion, or $3.54 billion net of the cash MaintainX held, and booked $3.12 billion of that, 85%, as goodwill. The filing also says Autodesk did not present pro forma results because the deal's effects "are not material" to its financial statements. If MaintainX alone accounted for that $35 million, the price would equal about 25 times its annualized quarterly revenue, TECHi calculates.

What does the 10-Q show about MaintainX?

Autodesk changed how it reports revenue by product this quarter. It created "Other products," which combines its media and entertainment software with what it calls Autodesk operations solutions, and restated the year-earlier figures to match. The media and entertainment part is Autodesk's older animation and visual-effects software business, which means the category mixes a mature product line with a newly acquired one. That category rose 35% to $135 million in the October quarter and 21% to $340 million over nine months, where the company credited both MaintainX and its enterprise business agreements, the multiyear contracts Autodesk signs with its largest customers. The year-earlier figures in the new category were restated, so the comparison is like for like.

The filing does not give MaintainX's revenue on its own. Its results have been included only since August 3, so the quarter holds about three months of MaintainX sales. The $35 million increase is the closest number the company provides, and it is not exact in either direction: other parts of the category could have moved, too.

Most of the price was recorded as goodwill rather than as specific assets. Of the $3.66 billion, $262 million went to developed technology, $216 million to customer relationships and $62 million to other net assets, with the rest recorded as goodwill. Autodesk said the allocation is not final.

What did Autodesk buy?

MaintainX sells mobile-first software that factories, builders and other operators use to run maintenance: work orders, inspections, asset tracking and frontline workflows. Autodesk's filing says the deal extends its reach from designing buildings and products into running them, "linking digital intent with real-world performance in a continuous closed-loop system," and that it expands its relationships with manufacturing and construction customers.

In size, the deal is large for Autodesk. The $3.54 billion net price equals about 42% of the revenue Autodesk expects for the whole fiscal year, using the midpoint of the $8.36 billion to $8.375 billion range it gave on Tuesday. In accounting terms, the company still calls it immaterial, because MaintainX's sales and costs are small against Autodesk's own.

Tuesday's earnings release mentioned MaintainX only once, in a footnote saying the forecasts include it. Those forecasts call for $2.725 billion to $2.75 billion of free cash flow this fiscal year. At the midpoint, the net price Autodesk paid equals about 1.3 years of that cash flow, TECHi calculates, which is one way to measure how much of the company's spending power went into a single purchase.

How fast is the rest of Autodesk growing?

Total revenue rose 16.6% to $2,160 million. Without the Other products line, revenue grew 15.5%, and if the whole $35 million increase is taken out of the total, growth would have been 14.7%, TECHi calculates. Either way, MaintainX and the rest of that line explain only a small part of the quarter: the Other products increase was 11% of the $307 million rise in total revenue.

The bigger engines were the established product families. Architecture, engineering and construction revenue rose 19% to $1,097 million, AutoCAD and AutoCAD LT 11% to $525 million and manufacturing 12.6% to $403 million, the filing shows.

The growth was broad across regions. Revenue in the United States rose 16% to $774 million, the rest of the Americas 25%, Europe, the Middle East and Africa 17% and Asia Pacific 12%. Over nine months, total revenue rose 17% to $6,140 million.

That matters for the outlook. As TECHi reported when Autodesk released results on Tuesday, the fourth-quarter forecast implies growth of 13.4% to 14.2%, slower than the year so far, even though MaintainX will again add revenue that was not there a year earlier.

What does the goodwill mean?

Goodwill is the part of a purchase price that cannot be pinned to specific assets, such as expected growth and the value of combining the businesses. Under U.S. accounting rules it is not written down gradually. Instead, Autodesk must test it for impairment at least once a year and take a charge if the business turns out to be worth less than its carrying value.

That makes MaintainX's growth the number to watch. With $3.12 billion of goodwill on the deal, a sharp slowdown in the business would raise the risk of a write-down later, while steady growth would leave it untouched. The 10-Q does not give any figure that would let outsiders run that test themselves.

How did Autodesk pay for it?

Autodesk used a mix of cash, a short-term loan and commercial paper. On August 3 it borrowed $1 billion under a 364-day term loan arranged with Citibank as agent, at a weighted-average rate of 4.58%, the filing says, and the loan was due to mature 364 days after the closing. At that rate, a full year of interest on $1 billion would be about $46 million, or about $11.4 million a quarter, roughly a third of the $35 million increase in Other products revenue.

The company also leaned on its commercial paper program, short-term unsecured borrowing that usually matures within months, so it has to be reissued or repaid from cash as it comes due. It had no borrowings under its main revolving credit line at October 31. Remaining performance obligations, the contracted revenue Autodesk has yet to recognize, stood at $7.59 billion, with $5.3 billion expected in the next 12 months.

How has the stock reacted?

Autodesk shares closed at $246.79 on Wednesday, 3.5% below Tuesday's close of $255.70, the first session after the results, according to Nasdaq data. They had closed at $234.71 on August 3, the day the deal closed, so the shares are 5.1% higher since then. That gain spans a weak November for technology stocks and two sets of quarterly results, so it says little about how investors value MaintainX on its own.

The 10-Q answers one question that Tuesday's release left open, and leaves another. It shows MaintainX is small next to Autodesk's $2.16 billion quarter, which is why the company calls its effect not material. It does not show how fast MaintainX itself is growing, which is the figure that would test the price Autodesk paid.

What to watch

  • The fourth-quarter report, and whether Autodesk breaks out revenue from its operations software.
  • The final purchase-price allocation, including any change to the $3.12 billion of goodwill.
  • How Autodesk refinances the $1 billion term loan, which comes due in August 2027.
  • How much commercial paper Autodesk has outstanding in its next filings, since that short-term borrowing helped pay for the deal.
  • Remaining performance obligations, which were $7.59 billion at the end of October.

data.title: Chip index heads for its second-worst November since 1999 with one short session left
data.description:
The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index has fallen 17.9% in November with one shortened trading session left, which puts it on track for its second-worst November since at least 1999. Only November 2000, when it fell 27.6%, was worse in Nasdaq's index history, and this month has already passed November 2008's 17.2% drop.

That ranking can still change on Friday, when U.S. markets close at 1 p.m. Eastern. TECHi calculates that the chip index would need to rise more than 0.84% from Wednesday's close to finish November ahead of 2008, while the Nasdaq Composite, down 7.28% for the month, would move from its third-worst November since 2000 to its fourth with a gain of just 0.37%.

How bad has November been for chip stocks?

The chip index closed at 10,688.80 on October 30 and at 8,774.86 on Wednesday, according to Nasdaq data. Measured month by month since late 1999, a 17.9% fall would be the 10th-worst of 324 complete months, and the second this year to drop more than 17%, after July's 20.6% slide.

Most of the months that were worse came from the dot-com collapse and the 2008 financial crisis. September 2001 fell 33.6%, November 2000 fell 27.6%, and October 2008 fell 22.0%. Only one of the nine months that were worse came after 2008: July of this year.

How did the month unfold?

It has not been a steady decline. The chip index fell 12.2% on November 5 alone, then recovered to 10,564.11 by November 11. From there it slid to a low close of 8,408.59 on November 20, after a 10.7% drop that day, leaving it 21.3% down for the month at that point.

The next three sessions swung both ways. The index jumped 14.0% on November 23, the day Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang, gave back 7.9% on November 24 and slipped 0.7% on Wednesday, after recovering most of an early fall of almost 8%. After swings that large, even a short session could shift the final figure by more than the margins that separate this November from 2008's.

Which AI hardware stocks fell the most?

The damage was uneven across the ten AI hardware stocks TECHi tracks. Through Wednesday they were down 21.8% on average for the month, with Marvell off 33.3%, Micron 32.0%, Dell 30.0% and Super Micro 29.3%, according to TECHi's calculations from Nasdaq closing prices. At the other end, Arista Networks was down only 2.9% and Broadcom 7.7%.

Micron, the memory maker, and the server builders Dell and Super Micro were among the hardest hit, along with Marvell, while Arista and Broadcom held up better. TSMC's U.S. shares were down 15.7%, close to the middle of the group.

How does the gap with the broader market compare?

Chip stocks have fallen much further than the rest of the Nasdaq this month. The chip index is 10.6% points behind the Nasdaq Composite in November, TECHi calculates, a wider gap than in either of the two worse Novembers. In November 2000 the chip index trailed the composite by 4.7% points, and in November 2008 by 6.4% points.

That difference matters for what kind of month this has been. In 2000 and 2008, the whole market was falling and chips fell a little more. This November, the selling has been concentrated in the stocks most tied to AI hardware, while the broader index has held up comparatively well.

What would Friday need to do?

For the chip index, the line to watch is a rise of 0.84%. Anything less leaves November 2026 behind only November 2000. A rise larger than that moves it to third, behind 2000 and 2008. To match November 2000 and become the worst November in the data, the index would need to drop another 11.8% in a half-day session.

For the Nasdaq Composite, the month is 7.28% lower, measured from its October 30 close of 25,437.00. That is worse than every November since 2008. Only 2000 and 2008 were worse since 2000, and the composite would have to fall 3.77% on Friday to overtake 2008. On the other side, a gain of more than 0.37% would lift it above November 2007's 6.93% decline, leaving it fourth.

Either way, the month stays the worst November since 2008 unless the composite rallies by more than 5.3% on Friday, the gain needed to finish better than November 2011's 2.39%.

What did futures show on Thursday?

Nasdaq-100 futures, which track the 100 largest non-financial companies on the Nasdaq and so carry the big chipmakers alongside software and consumer names, traded during the holiday. They were up 0.75% at 7:30 a.m. Eastern on Thursday, a hint rather than a forecast, because futures can move again before Friday's open and do not track the chip index one for one. Wednesday's session showed how far prices can travel in a day: the chip index fell almost 8% in the morning and recovered most of it by the close, as TECHi reported.

Thursday's Asian session also leaned higher. In Taipei, the main index rose 2.8% and five AI server and parts suppliers closed at the 10% daily limit after the U.S. trade representative's proposed tariffs left servers and chips out, as TECHi reported, though TSMC itself slipped 0.2%.

How does Nvidia's month compare?

Nvidia has fallen 27.0% in November, from $204.64 on October 30 to $149.30 on Wednesday. In the ten years of daily prices that Nasdaq publishes for the stock, only April 2022 was worse, at 32.0%, TECHi calculates from month-end closes.

This November is already worse than the two harshest months of the 2018 chip slump, October 2018's 25.0% drop and November 2018's 22.5% fall. The next marks are close by. A Friday gain of more than 2.58% would put November behind May 2019's 25.2% fall as well, making it the third-worst month in the decade. To match April 2022, the stock would need to drop another 6.8%.

Nvidia's path inside the month explains much of the chip index's. The stock fell through mid-November after Jensen Huang left as chief executive, then jumped when the board reinstated him on November 23, as TECHi reported. The gain from that day has since narrowed.

Why does a ranking matter?

Month-end figures are the ones that index providers and funds publish, and the ones most often cited later when a period is compared with others. A November that ranks second in a quarter-century of data will be quoted in that way, whatever happens in December.

The November figure also understates the damage over a longer stretch. October was a losing month too, with the chip index down 15.4%, so measured from its September 30 close the index is about 30.5% lower after two months, TECHi calculates. That two-month decline is larger than any single month in the index's Nasdaq history except September 2001, when it fell 33.6%. What any one holder has lost depends on when they bought.

What to watch

  • Friday's close at 1 p.m. Eastern, which settles November for the chip index, the Nasdaq and Nvidia.
  • Whether the chip index finishes above or below the 0.84% rise that separates second place from third.
  • Taipei and Seoul on Friday, which trade before the U.S. open.
  • December's first sessions, and whether the selling in AI hardware stocks carries into a new month.
  • Nvidia's quarterly report filing with the SEC, due in early December, for any update on the board's investigation.

data.title: Peter Thiel bought $122 million of Palantir stock at its November low, filings show
data.description:
Peter Thiel, a co-founder and director of Palantir Technologies, bought 850,100 of the company's Class A shares for about $122.3 million on Thursday, November 20, 2026, according to a Form 4 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission late on Tuesday. He paid an average of about $143.81 a share. Palantir closed that day at $143.49, its lowest close since its October 9 high of $209.05.

At 12:56 p.m. on Wednesday, Palantir's shares were at $161.42, so the purchase was worth about $137.2 million, a paper gain of about $15.0 million, or 12.2%, by TECHi's calculation. The same batch of filings shows chief executive Alex Karp and three other senior executives selling about $98.2 million of stock on November 20 and 23, mostly in automatic sales to cover taxes on vested shares. Thiel's purchase was larger than all of those sales combined, by about $24.1 million.

What did Thiel buy?

Class A common stock, in three blocks on November 20: 213,437 shares at an average of $142.91, 341,423 at $143.68 and 295,240 at $144.61, the filing shows. The shares are held by PLTR Holdings II LLC, of which Thiel is the sole beneficial owner. The filing reports 850,100 shares held after the purchases, but it notes that it does not describe all of Thiel's holdings and refers readers to Palantir's April 24 proxy statement and his Schedule 13G for those.

By TECHi's calculation, the three blocks cost about $30.5 million, $49.1 million and $42.7 million.

The purchases were made under a Rule 10b5-1 trading plan Thiel adopted on August 19, 2026, according to the filing's footnotes. Palantir closed at $175.19 that day. Thiel's average purchase price was about 17.9% lower than the price when the plan was set up.

How big was the purchase?

Large for one investor, small for the market. Palantir traded 36.6 million shares on November 20, according to Nasdaq's data, so Thiel's 850,100 shares were about 2.3% of that day's volume, by TECHi's calculation. Average daily volume in November through Tuesday was about 26.3 million shares. In dollars, the purchase was roughly the size of the four executives' sales combined, and larger by about $24.1 million.

Why does the trading plan matter?

Because it means the purchase was arranged in advance. A 10b5-1 plan lets an insider set up trades, or a formula for them, at a time when they do not have material non-public information, and then lets the trades happen later without the insider deciding each one. That protects the insider from claims of trading on inside knowledge. It also means the November 20 purchase cannot be read as a fresh decision that day; the plan's terms were fixed three months earlier.

A director buying more than $100 million of stock is still a different kind of trade from an executive selling shares to pay taxes, because the buyer is adding money rather than taking some out.

What did Karp sell?

Shares he had just received. On November 20, 975,000 of Karp's restricted stock units vested as Class B shares, according to his first filing. He converted 403,263 of them into Class A shares and sold them on November 20 and 23 in automatic sales to cover the required tax withholding, according to the filings. He converted and sold another 90,000 shares on November 20 under a 10b5-1 plan he adopted on March 12, 2026, and gave 58,562 shares to tax-exempt charities.

In total Karp sold 493,263 shares for about $75.1 million across the two days, an average of about $152.28 a share, by TECHi's calculation from the two filings. The second filing shows him holding about 6.43 million Class A shares directly afterward. Class B shares convert into Class A shares one for one, the filing says.

Who else sold?

Three other officers, all in automatic sales to cover taxes on vested stock units under their trading plans, according to their filings. Ryan Taylor, chief revenue officer and chief legal officer, sold 47,319 shares for about $7.3 million. Shyam Sankar, chief technology officer, sold 62,355 shares for about $9.6 million. David Glazer, chief financial officer and treasurer, sold 40,687 shares for about $6.2 million. Together with Karp, the four sold about $98.2 million.

What did the executives keep?

Most of their stakes. After the sales, the filings show Karp holding about 6.43 million Class A shares directly, Sankar about 795,000, Glazer about 639,000 and Taylor about 439,000. At Wednesday's price, Karp's directly held Class A shares alone were worth about $1.04 billion, and Sankar's about $128 million, by TECHi's calculation. Each sold less than a tenth of the Class A shares reported as held directly, by TECHi's calculation, so the selling does not suggest any of them are exiting. These figures cover only the shares reported on these filings, not every security each person may hold.

How has Palantir traded?

Sharply in both directions this month. The shares fell to $143.49 on November 20, down 31% from the October 9 high, then rose 11.1% on Monday, November 23, to $159.36, the day Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive and AI stocks rallied, as TECHi reported. They closed Tuesday at $161.18, according to Nasdaq's price history.

On Wednesday, Palantir was little changed at 12:56 p.m., up 0.1%, while the Nasdaq Composite was down 1.7%, after a much steeper fall at the open, as TECHi reported. The shares are down 9.2% this year and 22.8% below their October high. Their lowest close this year was $107.27 on June 25.

How should investors read the filings?

As two different kinds of trades. The executives' sales were mostly mechanical: when stock awards vest, part of the shares are sold to pay the tax, and those sales happen whatever the price. Karp's 90,000-share plan sale and Thiel's purchase were both set up in advance under trading plans, months before the trades.

What stands out is the size and direction of Thiel's trade. He bought on the day Palantir hit its lowest close in six weeks, and the stock has since risen about 12%. Because the plan was set in August, it is not evidence that he saw a bottom coming, but it does show a willingness to add a large position at prices well below where the shares traded when he set the plan up.

What does it mean for shareholders?

For holders, the purchase shows that a co-founder and director was willing to add more than $100 million to his position as the stock fell, even if the timing was set by a plan. The executive sales do not change their stakes much: Karp still holds millions of shares, and the tax sales are a routine part of how Palantir pays its leaders.

The stock's swings this month, from $209 to $143 and back to about $161, are a reminder that even with insiders buying, Palantir remains one of the most volatile large AI stocks.

What to watch

Further Form 4 filings under Thiel's trading plan, which would show whether the plan calls for more purchases. Karp's next vesting dates and the tax sales that come with them. Whether other directors or large holders follow with purchases of their own, which would show up in Form 4 filings within two business days. Palantir's fourth-quarter results, which will be the next test of its growth. TECHi's Palantir quote page carries the live price.
